Managing Seasickness on Your Shark Diving Tour

A shark diving trip should be one of the highlights of your time in Hawaiʻi—not two hours spent wishing you were back on land.

Seasickness is common, especially on smaller boats in the open ocean, but there are things you can do before and during your trip that may significantly reduce your chances of getting sick.

If you know you’re sensitive to motion, have gotten seasick before, or simply aren’t sure how your body will react to being offshore, a little preparation can make a big difference.

Medical Disclaimer: This guide is for general informational purposes only and is not medical advice. If you have questions about motion-sickness medication, medical conditions, pregnancy, medication interactions, or treatment for a child, talk with a physician or pharmacist before your trip.

Why Do People Get Seasick?

Seasickness is a type of motion sickness. It can happen when what your eyes see doesn’t match the movement your inner ear and body are sensing.

For example, you may be standing or sitting relatively still on the boat while your body is continuously moving with the waves. That conflicting sensory information can lead to nausea, dizziness, sweating, fatigue, and sometimes vomiting.

Some people are naturally more susceptible than others, and conditions can vary from one day to the next.

Even if you’ve never been seasick before, being on a small boat in the open ocean may feel different from being on a large ship, ferry, or calm-water boat ride.

Before Your Tour: How to Reduce Your Chances of Getting Seasick

The best time to think about seasickness is before you ever step onto the boat.

Once significant nausea begins, it can be harder to control. Preventative strategies—and motion-sickness medications when appropriate—generally work best when used before symptoms start.

Get a Good Night’s Sleep

Try to arrive well rested.

Sleep deprivation can make motion sickness worse, so the night before your tour probably isn’t the best time to stay out until 2:00 AM exploring Waikīkī.

Avoid Alcohol Before Your Tour

Alcohol can increase susceptibility to motion sickness and can also contribute to dehydration and fatigue.

If you think you may be prone to seasickness, consider skipping alcohol the night before your shark dive—or at the very least keeping it minimal.

A shark dive with a hangover is unlikely to improve either experience.

Stay Hydrated

Drink water before your trip and bring water with you.

Dehydration won't help if you begin feeling nauseated, and staying adequately hydrated is one of the simple things you can control before heading offshore. The CDC also recommends limiting alcohol and excessive caffeine when trying to reduce motion sickness.

Eat—But Don't Overdo It

Going offshore completely empty-handed and hungry isn't necessarily the answer.

A light meal or small amounts of food may be easier to tolerate than a large, heavy meal. Try to avoid especially greasy, spicy, or very heavy foods shortly before going out.

Consider Motion-Sickness Medication Before the Trip

If you've experienced motion sickness before—or you're concerned that you might—it may be worth talking with a pharmacist or healthcare professional about preventative medication.

Common motion-sickness medications include products containing ingredients such as dimenhydrinate or meclizine. Prescription options also exist.

The important thing to understand is that many motion-sickness medications work best before exposure to motion, rather than after you're already feeling sick. Some can also cause drowsiness or have other side effects and contraindications.

Follow the instructions for the specific medication you're using and talk with a healthcare professional if you're uncertain about what's appropriate for you.

A Special Note About Children

Do not assume that a motion-sickness medication appropriate for an adult is appropriate for a child.

Some medications require different dosing for children, some can cause unexpected reactions, and some motion-sickness medications should not be used in young children at all. Talk with your child's healthcare provider or pharmacist before giving them medication for motion sickness.

On the Boat: What to Do Before You Feel Sick

If you're concerned about seasickness, don't wait until you're nauseated to start paying attention to how you feel.

A few simple habits on the boat may help.

Look at the Horizon

One of the most commonly recommended techniques is to look outward toward the horizon or another distant, stationary point.

This gives your eyes a visual reference that better matches the movement your inner ear is sensing.

Keep Your Head Relatively Still

Constantly looking down, turning your head, or moving around unnecessarily can make symptoms worse for some people.

Keep your head relatively stable when possible and let your body move naturally with the boat.

Stay Off Your Phone

This is not the ideal time to answer email, read an article, scroll Instagram, or stare at your camera settings for ten minutes.

Looking down at a stationary object while your body feels the boat moving can increase the sensory conflict associated with motion sickness.

Take your photos, then look back up.

Get Fresh Air

Fresh moving air can help some people feel better.

If you're beginning to feel warm, clammy, or uncomfortable, getting into an open area with airflow may help.

Breathe Slowly and Normally

Controlled breathing may help reduce motion-sickness symptoms.

Rather than taking exaggerated deep breaths, try relaxing and breathing at a slow, comfortable, regular pace.

If You Start Feeling Seasick

Don't try to tough it out silently.

Tell the crew.

They spend a lot of time on the ocean and are accustomed to guests becoming seasick. Letting someone know early gives the crew an opportunity to help you before you're completely miserable.

Then:

  • Look toward the horizon.
  • Stop reading or looking at your phone.
  • Keep your head relatively still.
  • Get fresh air.
  • Sit or position yourself where the crew recommends.
  • Breathe slowly and regularly.
  • Sip water if you can tolerate it.
  • Try to relax rather than fighting every sensation.

Motion sickness can build quickly, so responding to the first signs is usually better than waiting to see whether they disappear.

What If I'm Already Really Seasick?

Sometimes prevention isn't enough.

If you're already very nauseated or vomiting, let the crew know and follow their instructions.

Try to rest and minimize unnecessary movement. Continue taking small amounts of fluid if you're able to tolerate them, particularly if you've been vomiting.

The CDC recommends maintaining adequate fluid and electrolyte intake when vomiting occurs.

And don't be embarrassed.

People get seasick.

It happens to experienced travelers, divers, fishermen, and people who have spent plenty of time on boats. Your body's response to motion isn't a reflection of how adventurous, tough, or comfortable you are in the ocean.

What About Ginger, Wristbands, and Other Seasickness Remedies?

You'll find many suggested seasickness remedies online, including ginger, acupressure wristbands, candies, supplements, and other products.

Some people swear by them.

Scientific evidence for many of these approaches is mixed or limited. The CDC notes that evidence for things such as ginger and dietary supplements is inconsistent, and controlled studies of acupressure bands have not shown them to be more effective than placebo.

That doesn't necessarily mean you can't use something you've found personally helpful. Just don't let an unproven remedy substitute for preparation or appropriate medical advice if you know you're highly susceptible to motion sickness.

If You Know You're Prone to Motion Sickness, Prepare Early

If you've been seasick before, get carsick easily, become nauseated on amusement park rides, or are generally sensitive to motion, don't simply hope for the best.

Research your options before the day of your shark dive.

Talk with a pharmacist or healthcare professional about motion-sickness prevention if necessary, understand when any medication you're using needs to be taken, and familiarize yourself with the techniques above.

Preparing before the tour can be the difference between spending the trip fighting nausea and being able to focus on why you came out in the first place:

swimming with sharks in the open ocean off Oʻahu's North Shore.

Quick Seasickness Checklist

The Night Before

  • Get a good night's sleep.
  • Stay hydrated.
  • Avoid or limit alcohol.
  • If you're using motion-sickness medication, make sure you understand when and how it should be taken.
  • Have everything ready so your morning isn't rushed or stressful.

Before Boarding

  • Eat an appropriate light meal rather than a very heavy or greasy one.
  • Drink some water.
  • Take any motion-sickness medication according to its directions or your healthcare provider's instructions.
  • Tell the crew if you're particularly concerned about seasickness.

On the Boat

  • Look toward the horizon.
  • Avoid prolonged phone use or reading.
  • Keep your head relatively still.
  • Get fresh air.
  • Breathe slowly and normally.
  • Tell the crew as soon as you begin feeling sick.

Medical Disclaimer

The information on this page is provided for general educational purposes and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any medical condition and should not be considered medical advice.

Medications used for motion sickness can cause side effects, interact with other medications, and may not be appropriate for everyone. Children, pregnant guests, people with existing medical conditions, and anyone taking other medications should consult an appropriate healthcare professional before using motion-sickness medication.

Always follow the instructions provided with any medication and the advice of your physician or pharmacist.
